statement: Build the domain model collaboratively between developers and domain experts (knowledge crunching) rather than having experts dictate software features or analysts hand specifications to programmers.
The waterfall hand-off from business experts to analysts to programmers fails because it lacks a feedback loop, so knowledge flows one way and never accumulates.

An iterative process that builds requested features without abstracting a model also fails to accumulate domain knowledge and never reaches the point where new features unfold as corollaries of older ones.
Bind the model to the implementation from the start: forge the link early with a working prototype and maintain it through every subsequent iteration.
Cultivate a language based on the domain model so that team members can take terms straight from the model and be understood without translation.
Make the model knowledge-rich: objects should carry behavior and enforce rules, not merely act as a data schema.
Distill the model by dropping concepts that do not prove central; when an unneeded concept is tied to a needed one, find a new model that separates the essential concept so the other can be removed.
condition: when a concept proves not useful or not central to the problem

statement: Use the spoken model-based language as a quick viability test of a proposed model: ease of expression signals a sound model while awkwardness signals a flawed one.
In early prototypes, avoid infrastructure such as persistence and user interface so the team can concentrate on domain behavior.
condition: during early model-exploration prototyping

statement: A good domain model consolidates synonyms and excludes facts irrelevant to the problem, giving newcomers a framework to organize information and learn faster.
Walk through concrete interaction scenarios with domain experts; when the model objects cannot carry an important scenario, brainstorm new objects or revise existing ones.
Domain models are never perfect and must evolve; they must remain practical, useful, and rigorous enough to make the application simple to implement and understand.
An important business rule hidden as a guard clause in an application method should be made explicit as a named domain concept so business experts can read and verify it.
Model a distinct business policy such as an overbooking rule as an explicit policy object (the STRATEGY pattern), making the rule clear and separate from the application logic.
condition: when the concept genuinely fits the meaning of a domain policy

statement: Do not apply elaborate design to every domain detail; focus effort on the important concepts and minimize or separate everything else.
Deep, useful models seldom lie on the surface; teams usually discard superficial early elements and discover subtle abstractions only through continued learning.
A fractured project language, where domain experts use their jargon and developers use their own design terms, leads to unreliable software whose parts do not fit together.
Translation between team sub-languages muddles model concepts, conceals schisms where people use the same term differently, and prevents the interplay of ideas needed for deep model insight.
Practice continuous learning to grow domain knowledge consciously, because projects constantly leak knowledge when people move on, teams reorganize, or subsystems are outsourced.
A domain model can serve as the core of a project's common language, supplying semantics tailored to the domain yet precise enough for technical development.

When knowledge crunching surfaces inconsistent business rules, collaboration with software experts is needed to clarify, reconcile, or place them out of scope, because software cannot fill gaps with common sense the way experts do.

Use the domain model as the backbone of a common language and commit the team to exercising that ubiquitous language relentlessly in all team communication, in diagrams, in writing, and especially in speech.

The vocabulary of the ubiquitous language should include class names, prominent operations, the rules made explicit in the model, the high-level organizing structures imposed on it, and the names of patterns commonly applied.
Persistent use of the ubiquitous language forces the model's weaknesses into the open, prompting the team to find alternatives to awkward terms and to introduce new words as gaps are discovered.
Recognize that any change to the ubiquitous language is a change to the model, so renaming a term must also update the class diagrams and the corresponding classes, methods, or behavior in the code.

Iron out language difficulties by experimenting with alternative expressions (which reflect alternative models), then refactor the code by renaming classes, methods, and modules to conform to the chosen model.

Domain experts should object to terms or structures that are awkward or inadequate to convey domain understanding, while developers should watch for ambiguity or inconsistency that will trip up the design.
Do not maintain two languages on a team: the linguistic division should never run between domain experts and developers, and rejecting that split (no shielding experts from the model) is required.
If sophisticated domain experts do not understand the core model, that is evidence the model is wrong rather than too abstract for them.
Refine the model by exploring with speech: describe scenarios out loud using the model's elements and interactions, because rough edges and awkward constructs are easy to hear.

A dialog enriched with explicit domain objects (such as Itinerary and Route Specification) conveys the domain expert's intent more concisely and precisely than one phrased in terms of tables, attributes, and procedures.
Have domain experts use the model language to write use cases and to specify acceptance tests, and reframe evolving requirements in the refined ubiquitous language.

Developers' technical jargon and users' specialized field jargon are legitimate extensions to the ubiquitous language, but these dialects must not contain alternative vocabularies for the same domain that reflect distinct models.
exception: technical or field-specific terms outside the application's modeled scope are allowed as extensions

statement: Use simple, informal UML diagrams of three to five central objects to anchor a discussion, rather than comprehensive diagrams of the whole model that overwhelm the reader so no one can see the forest for the trees.
A UML diagram cannot convey the meaning of the concepts it represents nor what the objects are meant to do, so these aspects must be filled in with natural-language text or conversation.
The model is not the diagram; the diagram exists to help communicate and explain the model, while the code serves as the authoritative repository of the design's details.
Prefer writing a text document illustrated with selective, simplified diagrams over a diagram annotated with text, keeping diagrams minimal so they communicate rather than overwhelm.

Written documents should complement the code and conversation rather than duplicate what code already does well, since code is an exact specification of behavior while other documents should illuminate meaning, large-scale structure, and core elements.

Judge whether a design document is alive by its interaction with the ubiquitous language: if its terms do not show up in conversation and code it is failing its purpose, and a document being left behind by the evolving language should be archived rather than maintained by sheer discipline.

Well-written code reveals the underlying model, but its message is not guaranteed accurate because method and variable names can be ambiguous, misleading, or out of date, so aligning code's behavior, intent, and message requires discipline.
To communicate effectively, the code must be based on the same language used to write the requirements and that developers speak with each other and with domain experts.

As the domain model reflects the most relevant business knowledge, application requirements become scenarios within that model, letting specifications be written more concisely because they no longer need to convey the business knowledge behind the model.
A single model should underlie implementation, design, and team communication; keeping separate models for these separate purposes poses a hazard.
Explanatory models used purely as teaching aids need not be object models, and it is generally best to avoid UML for them so as not to imply a false correspondence with the software design.
condition: when the model's role is education rather than driving design

statement: A domain model on paper is of little value unless it directly aids the development of running software.

Avoid splitting work into a separate analysis model and design model, because the analysis model gets abandoned once coding starts and a deadly divide opens in which insight from each activity does not feed the other.
Model-Driven Design discards the dichotomy of analysis model versus design model in favor of a single model that serves both purposes, demanding more of the chosen model.
When a model is not practical for implementation, or when it does not faithfully express the key domain concepts, search for a new model, making modeling and design a single iterative loop.

Design a portion of the software to reflect the domain model very literally so the mapping is obvious, and draw the design's terminology and basic assignment of responsibilities directly from the model.
Because the code becomes an expression of the model, a change to the code may be a change to the model, and its effect must ripple through the rest of the project's activities.

Tying the implementation closely to a model usually requires development tools and languages that support a modeling paradigm such as object-oriented programming; model-driven design has limited applicability in purely procedural languages like C.
exception: languages whose paradigm matches the domain (e.g. Fortran for mathematical models, Prolog for logic rules) can support model-driven design

statement: Only one model should apply to a particular part of the system throughout all aspects of development, from code to requirements analysis, even though different subsystems may use different models.
exception: different subsystems (bounded contexts) may each have their own model

statement: For model-driven design to pay off, the correspondence between model and design must be literal and exact within the bounds of human error.
The real breakthrough of object-oriented design comes not from using objects merely as fancy data structures but when the code directly expresses the concepts of a domain model.

Modeling an implicit concept (such as a bus grouping nets) as an explicit domain object scales to many operations and lets the core domain logic be unit-tested, whereas an inference-by-script approach is testable only through end-to-end file comparisons.

Make domain concepts explicit in the model rather than inferring them indirectly (for example through sorts and string matches), so behavior does not depend on incidental mechanisms like naming conventions.
An incisive model-driven design does not emerge in a single step; it takes several iterations of refactoring and knowledge crunching to distill the important domain concepts into a simple model.
Do not superimpose on the user interface an illusion of a model different from the domain model, because the mismatch causes confusion at best and bugs at worst unless the illusion is perfect.
Revealing the bones of a model-based design to the user gives more access to the software's potential and yields consistent, predictable behavior.
Quietly changing or discarding user data is unacceptable in most applications.
Software development is all design, so over-separating responsibility for analysis, modeling, design, and programming interferes with model-driven design.

If the people who write the code do not feel responsible for the model or do not understand how to make it work, the model becomes irrelevant to the software and refactoring weakens rather than strengthens it.
Any technical person contributing to the model must spend some time touching the code, and anyone responsible for changing code must learn to express the model through that code.

Programmers are modelers whether or not anyone intends it, because in a model-driven design changing the code changes the model, so the project should be arranged so that programmers do good modeling work.
Needing hands-on modelers does not forbid specialized team roles; the problem is specifically separating the two coupled tasks of modeling and implementation.
exception: specialized roles and high-level technical leadership are still legitimate

statement: Isolate the domain by decoupling domain objects from the system's other functions, so domain concepts are not confused with software-technology concepts or lost in the mass of the system.

In a layered architecture, any element of a layer depends only on other elements in the same layer or on elements of the layers beneath it, and upward communication must pass through an indirect mechanism.
Most successful architectures use four conceptual layers: user interface, application, domain, and infrastructure.

Keep the application layer thin: it coordinates tasks and delegates to domain objects but contains no business rules or knowledge, and holds no state reflecting the business situation (only task or progress state).

The domain layer represents business concepts, business situation information, and business rules, and is the heart of business software; fundamental business rules belong there, not in the application layer.

Concentrate all code related to the domain model in one layer, isolating it from user-interface, application, and infrastructure code, so domain objects are freed of displaying, storing, and task-management responsibilities and can focus on expressing the model.
Isolated layers are cheaper to maintain because they evolve at different rates and respond to different needs, and the separation also eases distributing layers across servers or clients.
When a lower-level object must communicate upward beyond answering a direct query, use architectural patterns such as callbacks or observers rather than a direct upward dependency.
condition: when the lower layer needs to notify a higher one beyond answering a query

statement: The infrastructure layer should not initiate action in the domain layer and should have no specific knowledge of the domain it serves; expose generic technical capabilities as services that the higher layers request.

Apply an architectural framework selectively to solve only the hard technical problems rather than as a one-size-fits-all solution, because judicious minimal use reduces coupling and keeps business objects readable and expressive.
Isolating the domain implementation is a prerequisite for domain-driven design, because the literal model-to-code correspondence is impractical when domain logic is mixed with other concerns.

The Smart UI approach (putting business logic directly into the user interface, backed by a shared relational database and rapid UI tools) is legitimate for simple projects dominated by data entry, with few business rules and a team not skilled in object modeling.
condition: when functionality is simple, business rules are few, and the team lacks advanced modeling skills

statement: The Smart UI is mutually exclusive with domain-driven design: it offers no reuse or abstraction of business rules and no graceful growth path to richer behavior, and migrating away requires replacing whole applications.

Domain-driven design pays off best for ambitious projects and requires strong skills; it is a common, costly mistake to adopt a sophisticated design approach the team is not committed to carrying through, or to build heavy infrastructure for a project that does not need it.

A team committed to model-driven design must design that way from the outset, taking even its first simple iterations as model-driven with an isolated domain layer, or the project will likely become stuck in a Smart UI.

For every traversable association in the model there must be a software mechanism with the same properties, and the design must specify a particular traversal mechanism whose behavior is consistent with that association.

Constrain associations as much as possible by imposing a traversal direction, adding a qualifier to reduce multiplicity, or eliminating nonessential associations, because general many-to-many bidirectional associations complicate implementation and communicate little.

Impose a traversal direction on an association when the application does not require traversal in both directions, because a bidirectional association forces the two objects to be understood only together and a directional bias usually reflects real insight into the domain.
condition: when application requirements do not call for bidirectional traversal
exception: retain both directions when bidirectionality is a genuine semantic characteristic needed by the application

statement: As constraints on associations (such as a qualifier reducing multiplicity to one) are discovered, embed them explicitly in both the model and the implementation, making the model more precise and the implementation easier to maintain.
Classify an object that is defined by a thread of continuity and identity running through its life cycle, rather than by its attributes, as an Entity.
A mistaken identity in a software system leads to data corruption and program errors, so an entity must be distinguishable from other objects even when they share the same attributes.

Make identity primary in an entity's model definition, keep its class focused on life-cycle continuity and identity, and orient its responsibilities, attributes, and associations around who it is rather than the attributes it carries.

Keep entities spare: strip the definition to the most intrinsic identifying characteristics plus only the behavior essential to the concept and the attributes that behavior requires, moving other behavior and attributes into associated objects.

Do not rely on the programming language's built-in identity operation (such as comparing memory locations) to track an entity's identity, because that mechanism is too fragile and is lost whenever the object is persisted, retrieved, or transmitted.

Define for each entity an operation guaranteed to produce a unique result that distinguishes it regardless of form or history, and let the definition of identity emerge from a careful understanding of the domain.

Identity is not intrinsic to a thing in the world but a meaning superimposed because it is useful, so the same real-world thing may or may not be represented as an entity depending on whether the application cares about distinguishing it.
An entity's identifying attribute or symbol must be guaranteed unique within the system however defined (even distributed or archived), and once assigned it must be designated immutable.
When no natural unique key exists among an entity's attributes, attach a generated symbol that is unique within the class as the identifier.
condition: when the object has no true attribute-based unique key

statement: When an application requires externally supplied identifiers, the users become responsible for supplying unique IDs and the system must give them adequate tools to handle the exceptions that arise.
condition: when the application requires an external ID

statement: If an ID-assigning operation or comparison does not correspond to a meaningful distinction in the domain it merely confuses matters, which is why identity matching often requires human input to make the final determination.
Classify an object that describes a characteristic of a thing and has no conceptual identity as a Value Object.

Do not assign artificial identity to all objects, because tracking identity on objects that do not need it hurts performance, adds analytical work, and muddles the model by forcing every object into the same mold.
Software design is a constant battle with complexity, so make distinctions in the model so that special handling is applied only where it is actually necessary.

Whether a concept such as Address is an Entity or a Value Object depends on the application's concerns: classify it as an Entity only when the application must distinguish and track that thing, otherwise as a Value Object.

When you care only about an element's attributes, model it as a Value Object that expresses the meaning of those attributes with related functionality, give it no identity, and treat it as immutable to avoid the complexities of maintaining entities.
The attributes that make up a Value Object should form a conceptual whole, so for example street, city, and postal code should be a single Address value rather than separate attributes of a Person.
For an object to be shared safely it must be immutable, meaning it can be changed only by full replacement, so that a change made by one holder does not silently corrupt another.

When an object passes one of its attributes to another object as an argument or return value, make the passed object immutable or pass a copy, to prevent the value being changed in a way that violates the owner's invariants.

Restrict sharing of value instances to the cases where it is most valuable and least troublesome: when saving database space or object count is critical, when communication overhead is low, and when the shared object is strictly immutable.
condition: when space saving is critical, communication overhead is low, and the object is strictly immutable

statement: A conceptual distinction in the model that cannot be declared explicitly in the implementation language is still useful; the lack of direct language support just means more discipline, reinforced by naming conventions, selective documentation, and discussion.

Design Value Objects as immutable whenever you can; allow a mutable implementation only for performance reasons such as frequent change, expensive creation or deletion, or clustering concerns, and a mutable value must never be shared.
exception: performance factors (frequent change, expensive create/delete, clustering) can justify a mutable, non-shared value

statement: Avoid unnecessary constraints in a model while explicitly defining the essential ones, so developers remain free to do purely technical performance tuning without changing meaningful behavior.

Eliminate bidirectional associations between two Value Objects, since without identity they are meaningless; if such an association seems necessary, reconsider whether the object actually has an unrecognized identity and is really an Entity.

When a significant domain operation does not conceptually belong to any Entity or Value Object, model it explicitly as a Service rather than forcing it onto an object where it would distort the object's definition.

Forcing an operation into an object where it does not fit costs the object its conceptual clarity and creates tangling dependencies, yet the more common mistake is giving up too easily and slipping toward procedural programming.

A good Service has three characteristics: it relates to a domain concept that is not a natural part of an Entity or Value Object, its interface is defined in terms of other domain-model elements, and the operation is stateless.
Name a Service for an activity (a verb) drawn from the ubiquitous language, define its responsibility and interface as part of the domain model, and make its parameters and results domain objects.
Use Services judiciously and do not let them strip Entities and Value Objects of all their behavior.

Distinguish domain Services from application and infrastructure Services: a domain Service embeds significant business rules and a meaningful domain term, whereas a technical Service should carry no business meaning at all.

Introduce medium-grained, stateless domain Services to encapsulate significant functionality behind a simple interface, which aids reuse, controls interface granularity, and prevents domain knowledge from leaking into the application or UI layers.

Provide access to a Service with the simplest mechanism that works (such as a singleton or doer object) and reserve elaborate distributed architectures for when there is a real need to distribute the system.
Cognitive overload, not just technical concerns, is the primary motivation for Modules, which should emerge as a meaningful part of the model and tell the story of the domain on a larger scale.

Treat low coupling and high cohesion as principles about concepts, not just code metrics: choose Modules that contain a cohesive set of concepts that can be understood and reasoned about independently of each other.
Give Modules names that become part of the ubiquitous language and reflect insight into the domain, because module names tell the next developer which classes to think about together.

Modules must coevolve with the model and code by being refactored alongside them; left unrefactored, module structures and names lag behind the classes and accumulate inertia that must be overcome by reorganizing based on where trouble spots lie.
When forced to trade off between conceptual clarity and technical coupling measures, favor conceptual clarity even at the cost of more references between modules or occasional ripple effects.
condition: when conceptual partitioning and low technical coupling cannot both be achieved

statement: Use packaging to separate the domain layer from other code, but otherwise leave domain developers as much freedom as possible to package domain objects in ways that support their model and design choices.

Do not let an infrastructure or tiered framework fragment a single conceptual domain object across multiple objects and packages, because that destroys object cohesion and leaves code that no longer transparently reveals the model.

Unless there is a real intention to distribute code on different servers, keep all the code that implements a single conceptual object in the same module, because splitting it for speculative flexibility sacrifices too much model-driven leverage.
exception: when there is a genuine, pressing need to deploy tiers on different servers

statement: Keep technical partitioning minimal: adopt only the partitioning rules essential to the technical environment or that genuinely aid development, because there is a limit to how much partitioning a mind can stitch back together.

Each concept in the domain model should map straightforwardly and obviously to an element of the implementation; when the objects, pointers, and retrieval mechanisms do not map cleanly, clean up the code, change the model, or both.
Resist adding anything to domain objects that does not closely relate to the concepts they represent, keeping other domain-related technical responsibilities and data out of these model objects.
Model-driven design does not require forcing everything into an object mold; other model paradigms such as rules engines are means to a model-driven design, not alternatives to it.

For most projects attempting model-driven design, use object-oriented technology as the core of the system, because its maturity, tooling, and community reduce the technical and staffing risks that come with novel paradigms.
condition: for the present, given current tool and community maturity
exception: domains that are intensely mathematical or dominated by global logical reasoning may fit other paradigms better

statement: Avoid an esoteric modeling paradigm that not enough developers can master and that nontechnical team members cannot grasp, because then they will not understand the model and the ubiquitous language will be lost.

Adopting an immature paradigm or technology risks costly setbacks, as a project that over-relied on a large-scale object database discovered when fine-grained object storage and tangled interdependencies caused scaling and contention failures; the lesson was to limit the web of relationships and decouple closely interrelated aggregates.

A domain model does not have to be an object model; model paradigms are conceived to match how people like to think about particular domains, and the model is shaped by the chosen paradigm so it implements well in that paradigm's tools.

Mix in another paradigm only when major parts of the domain genuinely belong to it; when interdependence is small, encapsulate the other-paradigm subsystem, and tolerate a few awkward objects rather than splitting the model when only a few elements are anomalous.
condition: when major parts of the domain naturally belong to different paradigms
exception: a few anomalous elements should be tolerated within the dominant paradigm rather than triggering a paradigm mix

statement: Model-driven design depends on an expressive implementation of the model constructs (objects, rules, or workflows); if the available tool does not facilitate that expressiveness, reconsider the choice of tools because an unexpressive implementation negates the paradigm's advantage.

When mixing nonobject elements into an object-oriented system, follow four rules of thumb: do not fight the implementation paradigm, lean on the ubiquitous language, do not get hung up on UML, and stay skeptical about whether the extra tool is pulling its weight.
Exhaust the options within the dominant paradigm before taking on the burden of mixed paradigms, since unconventional domain concepts can often still be modeled within the dominant paradigm.

A robust ubiquitous language, with names applied consistently across heterogeneous implementation environments, is the most effective tool for holding a multi-paradigm model together when no seamless tool connection exists.

Managing a domain object's life cycle poses two challenges, maintaining integrity throughout the life cycle and preventing the model from being swamped by life-cycle management, which are addressed respectively by Aggregates, Factories, and Repositories.
Define an Aggregate as a cluster of associated objects treated as a single unit for data changes, with a defined boundary marking what is inside and one Entity designated as its root.
Allow outside objects to hold references only to the aggregate root; entities inside the boundary have only local identity that needs to be distinguishable only within the aggregate.

Enforce all invariants of an aggregate at the completion of each transaction, while any rule that spans aggregates need not be kept up to date at all times and may be reconciled later by event or batch processing.
Obtain only aggregate roots directly through database queries; all other objects must be reached by traversing associations from the root.
Permit only transient references to an aggregate's internal members to be passed outside the boundary for use within a single operation, and never let an external object hold on to such a reference.

A delete operation must remove everything within the aggregate boundary at once, and when a change to any object inside the boundary is committed all invariants of the whole aggregate must be satisfied.
Make the aggregate root responsible for checking invariants and controlling all access to the objects inside its boundary, so it cannot be blindsided by changes to its internals.
Choose aggregate boundaries informed by the domain, particularly the relative frequency of change, so that high-contention points are left looser and strict invariants are kept tighter.

Locking a single fine-grained object (such as one line item) is inadequate to protect an invariant that spans the aggregate, because concurrent edits to separate members can together violate a whole-aggregate rule; lock or guard at the aggregate level instead.

Loosen a dependency that causes high contention (for example by copying a part's price into the line item that references it) so that changes to the shared object do not have to immediately affect existing aggregates, reflecting business reality and reducing contention.
condition: when the shared object is high-contention and its changes need not propagate immediately

statement: Make aggregate ownership reflect business practice, tying together the creation and deletion of objects that the business treats as a unit while keeping independently managed objects in separate aggregates.
When creating an object or an entire aggregate becomes complicated or exposes too much internal structure, encapsulate that creation in a Factory.
condition: when object or aggregate creation is complex or reveals internal structure

statement: Do not overload a complex object with responsibility for its own creation, and do not make the client assemble it either, because client-side construction breaches the object's encapsulation and couples the client to its concrete classes and rules, making refactoring harder.

Treat complex object creation as a responsibility of the domain layer even though it does not belong to the model objects themselves, adding factory constructs that are part of the domain design without corresponding to anything in the model.

Shift responsibility for creating complex objects and aggregates to a separate factory that provides an interface not requiring the client to reference concrete classes, and have it create entire aggregates as a piece while enforcing their invariants.

A good factory has two requirements: each creation method is atomic and enforces all invariants so it can only produce an object in a consistent state, and the factory is abstracted to the desired type rather than the concrete class created.

Place a factory where you want control, usually on the aggregate root as a factory method (or on a closely involved object), because a factory is tightly coupled to its product and should attach only to an object with a close natural relationship to it; otherwise create a standalone factory.

Prefer a bare public constructor over a factory when the class is its own type (not in an interesting hierarchy and not used polymorphically), the client cares about or needs the implementation, all attributes are available to the client, and construction is not complicated.
condition: when the class is not polymorphic, attributes are all available, and construction is simple

statement: Keep constructors dead simple and avoid calling constructors within constructors of other classes; reserve factories for complex assemblies, especially of aggregates, and note that even a public constructor must be atomic and satisfy all invariants.

Design a factory's method signatures so each operation is atomic with everything needed passed in at once, decide and standardize what happens when an invariant fails, and use the abstract types of arguments to limit coupling.

A factory may delegate invariant checking to its product, which is often best, but placing invariant logic in the factory is justified when the rules span an aggregate or when they would never apply during the product's active lifetime (for example immutable identity or value attributes).
condition: when invariants span an aggregate or never apply after creation

statement: Entity factories tend to take only the essential attributes required for a valid aggregate with details added later, whereas value-object factories must receive a full description because the immutable value comes out complete in its final form.

A factory used to reconstitute a stored entity must not assign a new tracking ID (which would lose continuity with the prior incarnation), so the identifying attributes must be part of its input parameters.
condition: when reconstituting a previously stored entity

statement: Reconstitution must handle an invariant violation more flexibly than creation: rather than simply balking as on new-object creation, it needs a strategy to repair the inconsistency, because an object that already exists in storage cannot be ignored.
condition: when reconstituting a stored object that violates an invariant

statement: Do not attempt to access all objects only by creation or association traversal, because forbidding query-based access forces an endless tangle of interconnections; use a database search to reach aggregate roots that are not convenient to find by traversal.

Treat whether to provide a traversal or depend on a search as a design decision that trades the decoupling of a search against the cohesiveness of an association, and choose the combination that makes the design comprehensible.

Accessing the database directly from client code tempts developers to bypass aggregates and object encapsulation, embedding domain rules in query code and reducing entities and value objects to mere data containers, which makes the model irrelevant.

For each type of object that needs global access, create a Repository that gives the illusion of an in-memory collection of all objects of that type, with add/remove and criteria-based selection methods that encapsulate the actual storage and query technology.
Provide Repositories only for aggregate roots that actually need direct global access, and keep the client focused on the model by delegating all object storage and access to the repositories.
Most objects should not be accessed by a global search; needing to search the database for a preexisting value object is a hint that it is really an entity whose identity has not been recognized.
exception: value objects with complex internal structure or enumerated values can warrant global access

statement: Repositories decouple application and domain design from persistence technology, communicate design decisions about object access, and allow a dummy in-memory implementation to be substituted for testing.

Even a repository designed with flexible (for example specification-based) queries should still allow the addition of specialized hard-coded queries, because frameworks that do not allow such contingencies distort the domain design or get bypassed by developers.

Although client code can ignore a repository's implementation, the developer must understand what happens under the hood because the performance implications of using encapsulated query behavior can be extreme.

Leave transaction control to the client: a repository ordinarily inserts and deletes but does not commit, because the client has the context to correctly initiate and commit units of work and transaction management is simpler when the repository keeps its hands off.

Keep Factories and Repositories distinct: a factory makes new objects while a repository finds old ones and gives the client the illusion that objects are in memory; reconcile the two by having the repository delegate object reconstitution to a factory.

Avoid combined find-or-create functionality, because the distinction between a new object and an existing one is usually important in the domain and a framework that transparently merges them muddles the situation.

Do not fight your frameworks: keep the fundamentals of domain-driven design, seek affinities between the framework's concepts and DDD concepts, let go of specifics when the framework is antagonistic, and if free to choose, pick frameworks harmonious with the design style you want.

When a relational database serves as the persistent store of an object model, do not let the data model and object model diverge far: sacrifice some richness of object relationships and some normalization to keep the mapping simple and transparent.
condition: when the database is primarily a store for the system's objects
exception: a deliberately distinct schema may be chosen when the database is shared with non-object software or evolves at a different rate

statement: Processes outside the object system should not access an object store directly, because they can violate the invariants the objects enforce and lock in the data model so it is hard to change when the objects are refactored.

For a relational database holding an object model, prefer simple directness, with a table row containing an object (plus aggregate subsidiaries) and a foreign key translating to a reference to another entity, and use the ubiquitous language so object names and associations correspond meticulously to the relational tables.

Choosing a database schema distinct from the object model is legitimate only as a conscious decision (for shared databases or differing evolution rates); when it happens by neglect, letting the database fall out of sync with the model, transparency is lost quickly.

Abstract a goal or criteria into a separate Specification object (such as a Delivery Specification) rather than loading it onto an entity, which keeps the entity simpler, lets diagrams safely suppress detail, and makes the model more expressive about what is undetermined.
Application-layer classes should act as coordinators only and not work out the answers to the questions they ask, leaving that work to the domain layer.

Classify each object as Entity or Value Object by asking whether it has an identity that must be tracked or is just a value being represented, consulting a domain expert when the means of identification is unclear.

Reuse an identifier the organization already assigns (such as an existing customer database ID) to establish continuity of identity between your software and other systems, rather than inventing a new one.
condition: when the business already maintains a usable identifier shared across systems

statement: An entity that has a one-to-one relationship with another and borrows its identity from that owner (such as a Delivery History tied to a Cargo) belongs inside the owner's aggregate boundary and need not be its own root.

Constrain an association's traversal direction to reflect what the business actually needs to track, which both captures domain insight and reduces the implementation (for example to a simple object reference).

Handle a circular reference in the model by avoiding holding the same information in two places that must be kept synchronized, for example replacing a maintained collection with a database query keyed on the root.
condition: when a model contains a circular or bidirectional reference

statement: Draw an aggregate boundary to sweep in everything that would not exist but for the root, but make an object the root of its own aggregate when its activity has meaning even when considered apart from that root.
Create a Repository only for an aggregate root that an actual application requirement needs to access directly, and do not add a repository or feature speculatively before it has been requested.
Cross-check model and design decisions by constantly stepping through application scenarios to confirm they solve the problems effectively.

When cloning an entity that is an aggregate root (using the Prototype pattern), copy everything inside the aggregate boundary, give the copy a fresh identity and a new empty history, but keep references to the same external entities rather than copying them.
condition: when creating a new aggregate-root entity from an existing one as a prototype

statement: Modeling and design is not a constant forward process; it will grind to a halt without frequent refactoring to take advantage of new insights and improve the model and design.

When entering events into one aggregate forces another aggregate into the transaction and creates contention, refactor by replacing the maintained collection with a repository query so the events can be added without integrity issues outside their own aggregate.
condition: when a frequent insert operation forces an unrelated aggregate into the same transaction

statement: Cleanly modeling values, entities, and their aggregates reduces the impact of later design changes, because such changes tend to be encapsulated within an aggregate boundary rather than rippling across the model.

Do not partition modules by design pattern or by technical scheme such as persistent versus transient objects, because such groupings tell the story of what the developer was reading rather than the story of the domain.
Partition modules by cohesive, broad domain concepts whose names tell the story of the domain and become part of the ubiquitous language.

When integrating with an external system built on a different model, insert a translating class (an Anticorruption Layer) that exposes only the features your application needs and reabstracts them in your own domain terms, rather than letting your application accommodate the other system's design.
condition: when interacting with an external system that was not written with your model

statement: Name an integration Service for its responsibility within your own system (for example Allocation Checker) rather than after the foreign system it talks to, using language to recast the problem along lines useful to your model.
Enforcing a business rule is a domain responsibility and should not be performed in the application layer; shift such rule enforcement into a domain object or service.

Assign responsibility for deriving a value to the object that knows the rules for the derivation rather than the object that merely holds the data, splitting those rules into a separate Strategy object when they vary by purpose.
condition: when the same data can be derived differently for different purposes

statement: An anticorruption layer conceived as a facade confines the ripple of changes in an external system to that single translating component, so changes in the other system reach only as far as the facade.

A stable component interface lets performance be tuned in the internal implementation (for example caching relatively static data to halve messaging in a distributed system), at the cost of extra complexity and keeping duplicated data up to date.
condition: when performance is critical in a distributed system

statement: The returns from refactoring are not linear: most refactorings yield marginal improvements that add up and fight entropy, but some of the most important insights arrive abruptly as a breakthrough.
A breakthrough to a deeper model is an event rather than a technique, and the challenge is to recognize what is happening and decide how to deal with it.

Removing an inappropriate constraint that the model imposed but the business did not (such as tying loan shares to facility shares) can collapse layers of special-case logic and resolve persistent defects at once.

Be suspicious of a model concept that is not a real domain term and that the domain experts do not understand, because it is likely an artifact invented from the team's incomplete understanding of the domain and should be removed.

When deciding whether to commit to a disruptive breakthrough refactoring, weigh the cost to regain current functionality, the slowdown of future progress without it, and whether it is the right long-term fit, recognizing the change is much harder once there is an installed base.
A breakthrough to a deeper model carries higher opportunity and higher risk than most refactorings, demands a major change to the design, and its timing may be inopportune.

Do not become paralyzed trying to force a breakthrough; instead push on the predictable levers that increase clarity, namely knowledge crunching, a robust ubiquitous language, making implicit concepts explicit, supple design, and distillation.

Keep making modest model-deepening improvements even within the same conceptual framework and stay watchful for the opportunity, because a real breakthrough often cascades into further breakthroughs as clearer vision exposes the next problem.
Deepen a model by recognizing a concept that is only hinted at in discussion or implicit in the design and representing it explicitly with one or more objects or relationships.

Dig out implicit concepts by listening to the team's language, scrutinizing awkwardness in the design, noticing seeming contradictions in experts' statements, mining the domain literature, and doing lots of experimentation.

Treat a vocabulary term that domain experts or developers use but that is absent from the design as a warning sign and an opportunity to improve the model by carving out that concept; this is not the naive notion that every noun becomes an object.

Making an implicit concept explicit as a model object (for example an Itinerary) yields a more expressive service interface, decouples components from database tables, reduces duplication, moves domain logic back into the domain layer, and expands the ubiquitous language.

Generalizing several special-case objects into one fundamental concept (such as collapsing distinct share types into a single Share Pie) simplifies calculations, makes them more expressive and combinable, and removes the need for special-case adjustment objects.
Dig for a missing concept in the most awkward part of the design: where procedures do complicated things that are hard to explain and where every new requirement seems to add complexity.

When a concept does not surface on its own, actively engage domain experts in the search, or generate candidate ideas with fellow developers and use the expert as a validator, watching for discomfort or recognition.

Treat contradictions among or within domain experts' statements as clues to a deeper model, contemplating how two statements could both apply to the same reality, though it is neither practical nor always desirable to reconcile every contradiction.
exception: some contradictions may be left in place rather than reconciled

statement: Consult the literature of the domain for fundamental concepts and conventional wisdom to gain a coherent starting point, then work with domain experts to distill the relevant part into something suited to the software, rather than reinventing established theory.
A developer who learns the theory of the domain (for example from a book) asks better questions and earns more engagement from domain experts.
Finding a good model takes much trial and error, so a modeler must not get attached to their own ideas; each change of direction embeds deeper insight and leaves the design more supple.
Trying to avoid all missteps in design produces a lower-quality result because it is based on less experience, and it can take longer than running a series of quick experiments.

Make an implicit constraint explicit by factoring it into a separate, intention-revealing method or object, which keeps the caller simple, names the rule so it can be discussed, and gives the constraint room to grow in complexity.

Factor a constraint out into its own object when warning signs appear: it requires data that does not otherwise fit the host object, related rules force duplication across unrelated objects, or much design conversation revolves around constraints that are hidden in procedural code.
condition: when a constraint distorts or obscures the host object's basic responsibility

statement: Do not make procedures a prominent aspect of the model in general, but represent a process that exists in the domain explicitly, expressing it as a Service for a complex algorithm or as a Strategy object when there is more than one way to carry it out.
Decide whether to make a process explicit by asking whether it is something the domain experts talk about or just part of the mechanism of the computer program.

Do not move business rules out of the domain layer into the application layer merely to relieve a host object, because that leaves behind a dead data object and the domain code no longer expresses the model.

When a business rule does not fit any obvious entity or value object and would swamp it, create an explicit predicate-like Value Object (a Specification) that determines whether an object satisfies the criteria, keeping the rule in the domain layer.

Use a Specification to unify validation, selection from a collection, and building-to-order, which are the same rule on a conceptual level, so a single consistent model serves all three even when the implementation must diverge.

Configure a Specification (often via a factory) with the information it needs from other sources such as account or policy data, which keeps that coupling out of the object being evaluated and preserves that object's basic responsibility.

Do not attempt a full implementation of logic programming in objects, because it is a major undertaking and so general it fails to communicate intent; instead create specialized predicate-like objects for the few special cases your rules fall into.

Treat a domain pattern as a solution to a programming problem that retains a model-driven design, not merely a neat UML idea; applying a pattern appropriately taps a body of accumulated experience and provides shared language to discuss the design.
Model-driven design demands the model stay in lockstep with the implementation but allows freedom to choose any implementation that faithfully captures the meaning of the model.

When implementing a specification-based query against a database, keep the rule declared in one place: express the repository's query generically (without capturing the rule) and let the specification control which query is used, so the essential definition stays in the specification.

Do not let database table-structure details leak into the domain layer; isolate them in a mapping layer that relates domain objects to relational tables, because duplicating that information hurts modifiability and maintainability.

Define a generator's interface in terms of a descriptive specification rather than procedural instructions, which decouples implementation from interface, communicates the output rules explicitly, keeps the request flexible in the client's hands, and makes the generator easier to test because the same specification validates the output.
condition: when a program generates or configures objects to meet criteria

statement: When asked to build a generator or solver, start with the validation problem, because making the rules explicit first yields a way to test the final implementation while keeping those rules in the domain objects.

Specify the postcondition of a complex service as an explicit assertion in its interface (for example, that each item's specification shall be satisfied or an exception thrown), which decouples the optimization mechanism from the rest of the design while keeping the rules in the domain.

Clear a development logjam between teams with a model-driven prototype of a key component, even an incomplete one, because when implementation is decoupled from interface any working implementation lets the rest of the system proceed in parallel and closes the feedback loop until a better implementation replaces it.
condition: when one team must wait on another's component or on full integration

statement: A well-characterized interface with assertions lets a sophisticated implementation be swapped in for a prototype with easy integration, because the application was written against the same interface and assertions throughout.

Software must serve developers as well as users: when complex behavior lacks a clean design, fragility and duplication place a ceiling on the richness of behavior feasible to build and stop refactoring and iterative refinement.
Aim for a supple design that is a pleasure to work with and inviting to change, so a project accelerates as development proceeds rather than getting weighed down by its own legacy.

Beware over-engineering justified as flexibility, because excessive layers of abstraction and indirection usually get in the way; empowering designs are typically simple, though simple is not easy and requires model-driven design joined with a rigorous design style.

A supple design must serve both the client developer (revealing a deep model usable through a minimal set of loosely coupled concepts with predictable results) and the developer changing it (easy to understand, with changes bending at flexible points and transparently obvious effects).
Do not expect an entire large program to be supple; hone the most crucial, intricate parts to a supple design when complexity is holding back progress.
condition: when complexity in a crucial part is holding back progress

statement: Name classes and operations to describe their effect and purpose without reference to the means by which they achieve it (an Intention-Revealing Interface), and make those names conform to the ubiquitous language so team members can infer their meaning without reading the internals.

If a developer must consider a component's implementation in order to use it, the value of encapsulation is lost, and inferring an operation's purpose from its implementation can corrupt the conceptual basis of the design.
Write a test for a behavior before creating it, to force your thinking into client-developer mode so the interface is shaped by how it will be used.

In a domain's public interfaces, state relationships, rules, events, and actions but not how they are enforced or carried out, encapsulating the tricky mechanism behind abstractions that speak in terms of intentions rather than means.
Drive interface design by writing the test the way you would want to talk to the objects from a client application, then refactor the class to make that test pass.

Place as much program logic as possible into side-effect-free functions that return a result with no observable change to system state, because functions can be combined and nested safely, return the same value each time, and are much easier to test.
Strictly segregate commands, which modify observable state, into very simple operations that do not return domain data, keeping them separate from queries and calculations.
Eliminate a side effect by moving complex calculation into an immutable Value Object and deriving a new value object as the result, rather than modifying an existing object's state.
condition: when a concept fitting the calculation's responsibility presents itself

statement: Modifying an argument passed to a method is a particularly risky kind of side effect and should generally be avoided.

State the post-conditions of operations and the invariants of classes and aggregates as assertions, and where the language cannot express them directly, capture them as automated unit tests or in documentation.
Because assertions describe state rather than procedures they are easier to analyze and test, and a trusted post-condition lets a developer use an operation without understanding how it works.

When side effects are defined only implicitly by their implementation, designs with much delegation become a tangle of cause and effect that can only be understood by tracing execution, defeating encapsulation, abstraction, and polymorphism.
Seek models with coherent sets of concepts that lead a developer to infer the intended assertions, accelerating the learning curve and reducing the risk of contradictory code.

When a logically consistent model turns out to be unsuitable for the application's requirements, treat the awkwardness as a sign of missing concepts and look for a new model rather than just documenting a counterintuitive post-condition.
exception: sometimes a non-intuitive property is genuinely the best answer and must be documented

statement: Decompose design elements into cohesive units guided by intuition of the important divisions in the domain (its conceptual contours), rather than by cookbook rules of fine, coarse, or uniform granularity which do not work as general rules.

Implement an operation at the level where it has a coherent meaning in the domain (a whole value), and clump detail that the software's users do not need to dissect, to avoid clutter and irrelevant options.

Treat localized refactorings that do not shake multiple broad model concepts as an indicator of model fit, and treat a requirement that forces extensive changes to the breakdown of objects and methods as a message that the domain understanding needs refinement.

Design aligned with the domain's conceptual contours accommodates unanticipated change more gracefully than a design made artificially versatile, because shared underlying concepts let new requirements connect naturally without duplication.

Treat every dependency (associations, argument types, return types) as suspect until proven fundamental to the concept behind the object, because interdependencies make models hard to understand, test, and maintain and they pile up quickly.

Factor the most intricate computations into Standalone Classes (often value objects with zero nonessential dependencies) so they can be studied and tested alone, which significantly eases understanding the surrounding module.

Aim to eliminate nonessential dependencies rather than all dependencies, and do not dumb down the model by arbitrarily reducing everything to primitives, because implicit concepts add to mental load as much as explicit references.
exception: a dependency that is fundamental to the concept, or a tightly coupled pair whose multiple operations clarify the relationship, should be kept

statement: Where it fits, define an operation whose return type is the same as the type of its argument(s) (closure of operations), because such a closed operation provides a high-level interface without introducing any dependency on other concepts and can be chained or combined.
condition: where the operation naturally returns the same type it operates on

statement: Look for closure of operations mainly among Value Objects rather than Entities, because an entity's life cycle has domain significance so a new one cannot simply be conjured up as the result of a computation.
exception: some operations are closed under an entity type, such as asking an Employee for its supervisor

statement: Even a partially closed operation, where only the argument or only the return type matches the implementer and the extra type is a primitive or basic library class, gives many of the benefits of closure by not adding to the developer's mental load.

Declarative design, where a precise description of properties is itself executable and controls the software, is the ideal of model-driven design but has real pitfalls: declaration languages too weak to extend, and code generation that makes regeneration destructive to handwritten code.

The greatest value from declarative frameworks comes when a narrowly scoped framework automates a particularly tedious and error-prone aspect such as persistence and object-relational mapping, while leaving developers complete freedom to design.
A declarative approach is corrupted when developers bypass it (likely when the system is hard to use or overly restrictive), so everyone must follow the framework's rules for the benefits to hold.

A supple design built from intention-revealing interfaces, side-effect-free functions, and assertions already enables a declarative style of client code, because the elements are combinable, communicate their meaning, and have characterized or no observable effects.

Make specifications combinable with logical AND, OR, and NOT operators (closed under predicates) so complex rules can be built declaratively from simple specification elements, increasing the expressiveness of the code.

Using a pattern does not mean building features you do not need; implement only the capability required now (for example only the AND operator on specifications) and add the rest later, as long as the concepts do not get muddled.

The same pattern and model can underlie very different implementations, so choose an implementation whose trade-offs (object count, memory, speed, required developer skill) fit your circumstances, keeping the model faithful to the domain's key concepts.
Do not try to make an entire large system supple at once; choose targets and carve off subdomains, which leaves both the extracted module and the remaining part cleaner.
Make a big impact on one area by making a part of the design really supple rather than spreading your refactoring effort thin across the whole system.

Draw on established formalisms when you can, adapting long-refined conceptual systems such as accounting or mathematics, because they offer well-developed entities and rules that map easily to a deep model and a supple design.
Look for and dig out specialized math hidden in a domain, because specialized math is clean, combinable by clear rules, and people find it easy to understand.

When most rules and calculations apply to a group of objects rather than to single ones, that points to a missing whole-concept (such as a Share Pie aggregating shares); making that concept explicit lets the rules and calculations be expressed more succinctly.

Refactor a method that both calculates a result and modifies state into a separate side-effect-free calculation function and a simple command, so client code first computes the distribution and then applies it.
The hands-on experience of implementing a new design often triggers a new insight into the model itself, so treat implementation as part of the modeling cycle rather than a separate downstream step.

Centralizing complex calculation in an immutable value object with closed, side-effect-free operations lets client code be written in a declarative style that reads like a conceptual definition of the business transaction rather than a calculation.

Easy recombination and communicative code result from four combined properties: complex logic encapsulated in value objects with side-effect-free functions, simple state-modifying operations characterized by assertions, decoupled model concepts (often closed operations), and a familiar formalism that makes the protocol easy to grasp.

Prefer adapting a familiar formalism (such as arithmetic) over inventing an original protocol, because an original protocol must be both invented (a difficult, uncertain task) and learned by everyone, whereas a familiar system is recognized and does not mislead people as long as the design stays consistent with its rules.

Use analysis patterns as expressive, implementable starting points that carry accumulated cross-project experience and cut through costly trial and error, but treat them as guides to refactor and experiment from, not out-of-the-box solutions.

The most useful analysis patterns combine model insights with extensive discussion of design directions and implementation consequences, because discussing model ideas out of implementation context risks reopening the deadly divide between analysis and design.

Validate a borrowed analysis-pattern concept against your domain with an expert and discard the parts that do not fit (for example a Transaction tying accrual to payment that the business keeps separate), keeping only what genuinely matches.

When infrastructure forces a compromise (such as an object-relational mapping standard requiring concrete subclasses per table), make the calculated compromise and move on without letting it throw the model-driven design off course.

Some parts of a program that look like complicated application code (such as a nightly batch script) actually hide domain logic, and analysis patterns can reveal these blind spots and let that logic be moved into an explicit domain model.
Tame a tangle of cross-account dependencies by making the dependency rules explicit as objects (Posting Rules), each triggered by a new entry and deriving an entry into an output account.

Give each set of dependency rules one clearly defined point of initiation and responsibility for identifying its inputs, and add the distinct firing-mode terms to the ubiquitous language, since that vocabulary eliminates ambiguity and guides decisions as much as the model objects do.

When you adopt a term from a well-known analysis pattern, keep the basic concept it designates intact even as the superficial form changes, and if the model's definitions evolve away from it, change the names too so the ubiquitous language stays honest.

An analysis pattern rarely answers your particular need exactly, but it offers valuable leads, cleanly abstracted vocabulary, and guidance about implementation consequences that saves pain down the road.

Reapplying organized knowledge through analysis patterns differs from reusing code, because an analysis pattern is a kit of model fragments focused on the most critical and difficult decisions and their downstream consequences rather than a complete working whole.

Sometimes a pragmatic placement of responsibility differs from the conceptually cleanest one for the sake of obvious, direct code; record the conceptual ideal so later refactoring and deeper insight can recover it without losing clarity.
To use a design pattern in domain-driven design, view it on two levels simultaneously: as a technical design pattern in the code and as a conceptual pattern in the model.
Only a subset of published design patterns work as domain patterns, namely those that correspond to general concepts emerging in many domains rather than purely technical solutions.

Factor the varying part of a process into a separate Strategy (Policy) object, separating a rule from the behavior it governs, so that as a domain pattern it expresses a meaningful process or policy concept rather than merely allowing algorithm substitution.

Replacing conditionals scattered through a process with an explicit Strategy passed as a parameter lets the process handle all requests uniformly, makes a fundamental domain rule explicit, and yields clear, easily testable, extensible behavior.

When a domain Strategy corresponds to an actual business strategy or policy it becomes more than an implementation technique, yet all the design pattern's technical consequences still apply, such as implementing strategies as stateless shared objects to reduce object count.

Apply Composite by defining an abstract type that encompasses all members, having containers return aggregated information about their contents and leaves return their own values, so clients deal with the abstract type without distinguishing leaves from containers.
condition: when there is a true whole-part hierarchy whose parts are the same conceptual type

statement: When applying any design pattern in the domain, the first concern is whether the pattern idea genuinely fits the domain concept, for example whether there is a true whole-part hierarchy and an abstraction under which all the parts truly are the same conceptual type.

Push a Composite to its operational level so that it offers the same behavior at every structural level and meaningful questions can be asked of small or large parts; that rigorous symmetry is the key to the pattern's power.
Apply a design pattern only when it is actually needed, not speculatively for options the design does not yet require.

A design pattern qualifies as a domain pattern only if it says something about the conceptual domain, not merely solving a technical problem; for example Flyweight is an implementation option for value objects with no correspondence to the model, unlike Composite which applies to both model and implementation.
Refactoring toward deeper insight rests on three focuses: live in the domain, keep looking at things a different way, and maintain an unbroken dialog with domain experts.

Initiate refactoring toward deeper insight not only from awkward code but also when the model's language seems disconnected from the domain experts, when new requirements do not fit naturally, or when learning reveals a more lucid model.

Explore a model problem with a small self-determining team of four or five (including a domain expert when there are subtleties) brainstorming in short sessions of half an hour to ninety minutes, spaced over a few days, narrowing scope if stuck, to refine the ubiquitous language before coding the result.

Feed the knowledge-crunching process with prior art from domain books, analysis patterns, design patterns, and established formalisms, treating them as inputs to combine with local knowledge rather than cookbook recipes.

Do not wait until a refactoring can be completely justified, because by then the project is already incurring heavy costs and the postponed change is harder to make as the target code becomes more elaborated and embedded.

Refactor when the design does not express the team's current understanding of the domain, when important concepts are implicit and you see a way to make them explicit, or when you can make an important part of the design suppler.

Temper aggressive refactoring with limits: do not refactor the day before a release, do not introduce supple designs that are mere technical virtuosity failing to cut to the domain core, and do not introduce a deeper model that a domain expert would not use.

Treat a sudden, obvious inadequacy in the model as an opportunity rather than only a crisis, because it signals the team has reached a new level of understanding from which a far better model can be conceived.

Combining code based on two different implicit models of the same term (such as two teams' conflicting Charge objects) produces unreliable software, and the root of the problem lies in team organization and the absence of a process to detect divergence, not just in the code.

The most fundamental requirement of a model is internal consistency (unification): every term has the same unambiguous meaning and no rules contradict, because a model is meaningless unless it is logically consistent.

Total unification of the domain model for a large enterprise system is not feasible or cost-effective, so allow multiple models to develop while making conscious choices about which parts may diverge and how they relate.

Do not overreach by trying to unify all software in a large project under a single model, because it risks attempting too many legacy replacements at once, coordination overhead exceeding the team's ability, specialized requirements being unsatisfied, and a model bloated with complex options.

Model divergence arises as much from political fragmentation, differing management priorities, and team organization as from technical concerns, so even with no technical barrier to integration a project may still face multiple models.

Explicitly define the Bounded Context within which a model applies, setting its boundaries in terms of team organization, usage in specific parts of the application, and physical manifestations such as code bases and database schemas, and keep the model strictly consistent inside while not being distracted by issues outside.

Drawing an explicit context boundary keeps the model pure and potent where it applies and avoids confusion when attention shifts elsewhere, while making any integration across the boundary an explicit translation to be analyzed.
Bounded Contexts are not Modules: modules organize elements within one model and their separate name spaces inside a single context can actually make accidental model fragmentation harder to spot.

When two teams intend to share a model but have no demarcation and no process to hold it together, stop sharing code until the relationship is defined, because informal sharing across an undefined boundary is a real risk.
condition: when teams share objects without an explicit bounded-context relationship

statement: Treat a confusion of language as the early warning of unification breaking down within a context, and watch for the two categories of damage from combining distinct models: duplicate concepts and false cognates.

False cognates, where two people use the same term or object believing they mean the same thing but do not, are more insidiously harmful than duplicate concepts, causing teams to step on each other's code, contradictory databases, and communication confusion.

Institute Continuous Integration within a bounded context, merging all code and other implementation artifacts frequently with automated tests to flag fragmentation quickly, and relentlessly exercising the ubiquitous language to keep a shared view of the evolving model.

Continuous integration operates on two levels, the integration of model concepts through constant communication and the integration of the implementation through a reproducible merge/build/test process, and effective processes cap the lifetime of unintegrated changes to a reasonably small limit.

Apply continuous integration only within a bounded context (for any context larger than a two-person task); design issues with neighboring contexts, including translation, do not have to be handled at the same pace.

Create a Context Map by identifying each model in play (including the implicit models of non-object-oriented subsystems), naming each bounded context and putting those names into the ubiquitous language, and describing the points of contact and the explicit translation between contexts.
Avoid code reuse between bounded contexts, since integration of functionality and data between them must go through a translation.

Map the existing terrain as it actually stands before attempting transformations, describing the relationships you genuinely find rather than forcing them to a pattern name, and ensure the context map is shared and understood by everyone on the project.

Until you have an unambiguous context map placing all work into some bounded context with explicit relationships, change only the outright contradictions, and never change the map until the change in reality is actually done.

When a sub-team has a well-founded technical need for a different conceptual organization (such as an optimized network model for routing), yield by creating separate bounded contexts each with its own model rather than dogmatically imposing one model.
condition: when a distinct model is needed for performance or to use established algorithms

statement: Translating between two bounded contexts requires mapping only the specific translations actually needed, not everything in both models, and some translations are legitimately impossible or ambiguous but harmless when not required.
Implement translation between contexts in a dedicated translator object that both teams collaborate to maintain and to test, after which they can otherwise work independently.

Test the contact points with other bounded contexts particularly thoroughly, because such tests compensate for the subtleties of translation and the lower communication at boundaries and act as an early-warning system, especially when you depend on a model you do not control.

Give bounded contexts names that enter the team's ubiquitous language, ensure everyone can recognize the context of any piece of code, and work the context map into discussions by referring to model and context names rather than to which team owns the code.

Choose a relationship pattern between bounded contexts based on the level of control you have over the other model, the level and type of cooperation between teams, and the degree of integration of features and data.

When the overhead of full continuous integration across two teams is too high, designate a Shared Kernel: an explicitly agreed subset of the model and its code or database design that has special status and is not changed without consulting the other team.
condition: when functional integration is limited but some sharing is valuable

statement: Integrate a shared kernel less often than the pace of continuous integration within each team, running the tests of both teams at each kernel merge, because all of both teams' tests must pass when the kernel changes.
