At some point, regardless of retries, you will have to give up trying to process a message, because building reliable systems with distributed messages is hard.
Making explicit the requests that a system can respond to by giving each a name and its own data structure is a fundamental design step.

Creating a microservice per database table with HTTP APIs as CRUD interfaces over anemic models is the most common initial approach to service-oriented design, but it works only for very simple systems and quickly degrades into a distributed big ball of mud.

When two things have to be changed together they are coupled, and a failure cascade in which every part of the system must work at the same time for any part to work is temporal coupling, whose probability of some part being degraded rises as the system grows.

Connascence describes types of coupling, and you should aim for strong connascence locally and weak connascence at a distance; replacing RPC-style calls with events swaps the stronger Connascence of Execution and Timing for the weaker Connascence of Name, where components need only agree on an event's name and its fields.
You can never completely avoid coupling except by not talking to any other software, so the goal is to avoid inappropriate coupling rather than all coupling.

Think in terms of verbs, not nouns, because the domain model models a business process; build a system for ordering and a system for allocating rather than a system for orders and a system for batches.

Like aggregates, microservices should be consistency boundaries, so accept eventual consistency between services, let each service accept commands and raise events, and have other services listen to those events instead of relying on synchronous calls.

To avoid the distributed ball of mud, integrate systems with asynchronous messaging instead of temporally coupled HTTP API calls, receiving external messages from upstream systems and publishing events for downstream systems to consume.

Asynchronous event integration lets systems fail independently, so you can still take orders while the allocation system is degraded, and it reduces coupling strength so you can change the order of operations or add steps locally.
A message broker takes messages from publishers and delivers them to subscribers, with options including Event Store, Kafka, RabbitMQ, or a lightweight Redis pub/sub channel.

A message-queue event consumer or publisher is another thin adapter like the web framework: the consumer deserializes JSON into a command and passes it to the service layer, and the publisher converts internal domain events into public messages.
Keep the distinction between internal and external events clear, since not all internal events should be upgraded and published externally, and apply validation to outbound events in particular.

Event notification implies a low level of coupling and is simple to set up, but it becomes problematic when a logical flow runs across several event notifications, because that flow is not explicit in any program text and so is hard to see, debug, and modify.

Reads (queries) and writes (commands) are different and should have their responsibilities segregated; the domain model with its constraints, Unit of Work, Aggregate, and Domain Events patterns is a set of tools built for writing data.

The read side and write side of a system differ: reads are simple, highly cacheable, and can be stale, whereas writes carry complex business logic, are uncacheable, and must be transactionally consistent.
Make reads eventually consistent to make them perform better, taking advantage of the fact that a slightly stale read is usually harmless while an inconsistent write corrupts orders.
The write-side machinery of the service layer, unit of work, and domain model buys nothing for reading data and is just bloat for read operations.
By command-query separation, a function should either modify state or answer a question but never both, so that you can always ask whether the lights are on without flicking the switch.

The Post/Redirect/Get pattern applies command-query separation at the web layer by separating the write and read phases of an operation, which avoids double-submitted data and broken bookmarks of a results page.
Split your read-only views from your state-modifying command and event handlers, keeping reads in a separate module, which is worthwhile even if you do not go to full CQRS.
Test a view with at least one integration test whose setup goes through the public entrypoint, the message bus, so the test stays decoupled from any implementation detail of how data is stored.
A domain model designed primarily for writes is awkward to reuse for reads, forcing extra helper methods and Python-side looping and filtering that the database could do far more efficiently.
For a simple CRUD app, reads and writes are closely related so you need neither a domain model nor CQRS, but the more complex the domain, the more likely you need both.
exception: when the app is a simple CRUD app with closely related reads and writes

statement: The SELECT N+1 problem is a common ORM performance problem where retrieving a list issues an initial query for the objects' IDs and then a separate query per object for its attributes, especially with foreign-key relationships.

A fully normalized relational schema is a good way to ensure write operations never cause data corruption, but retrieving data with lots of joins can be slow, so it is common to add denormalized views, read replicas, or caching layers.

Once you reach the limits of what indexes can do, building a denormalized copy of your data optimized for reads is a reasonable approach, since even with well-tuned indexes a relational database spends a lot of CPU on joins and the fastest queries are single-key lookups with no joins.

Read-only stores can be horizontally scaled out because there is no limit to the number of clients concurrently reading, unlike writes which need row locks, so if you struggle to scale a complex data store, ask whether you could build a simpler read model.
Keep a denormalized read model up to date with event handlers that insert on allocation and delete on deallocation, instead of database views or triggers, which would tie you to your database.

A read model that fails to update because of a bug or outage is another case of events failing independently, and you can rebuild it by querying the current write-side state and replaying each item through the read-model update handler.

Updating a read model through event handlers makes it easy to change the read model's storage implementation later, for example swapping to Redis, while the same implementation-decoupled integration tests keep passing.

When read operations act on the same conceptual objects as the write model, using the ORM, adding read methods to your repositories, and using domain classes for reads is just fine; reach for a separate read store only when the read entities are conceptually different.

Declare a handler's dependencies explicitly, for example passing in the unit of work or a send-mail callable, rather than importing them implicitly, because explicit dependencies make tests easier to write and manage and are an application of the dependency inversion principle.

Managing dependencies implicitly by import and monkeypatching forces you to call mock.patch in every test that could trigger the side effect and tightly couples the tests to the implementation, such as the exact import path.
Declaring explicit dependencies is strictly unnecessary and makes application code marginally more complex, but the trade-off buys tests that are easier to write and manage.

Use a Composition Root, a single bootstrap script, to perform manual dependency injection, rather than putting the responsibility for passing dependencies to each handler onto the message bus, which would violate the single responsibility principle.

Compose a handler with its dependencies ahead of time using closures or functools.partial so it can be called later with the dependencies already injected, noting that closures use late binding of variables which can confuse if any dependency is mutable.
condition: when working in Python

statement: A bootstrap script should declare default dependencies while allowing overrides, perform one-time initialization, inject the dependencies into the handlers, and return the configured message bus.
Use the bootstrap function's argument defaults as the single place to define production defaults, but default a dependency to None instead when its construction has side effects.
exception: when constructing the dependency has side effects

statement: Structure the application to do dependency injection in a single place, the handler functions, in which case both a super-manual inline-partial approach and a signature-inspecting approach work fine.
Reach for a real dependency injection framework only if you need to do DI at multiple levels or have chained dependencies whose dependencies have their own dependencies.
exception: when DI is needed at multiple levels or dependencies are chained

statement: Gather one-time setup activities such as dependency injection, ORM mapper start-up, and logging configuration into a bootstrap script, which is also the place to provide sensible adapter defaults and the single place to override adapters with fakes in tests.

To build an external dependency as a proper adapter, define its API with an abstract base class, implement the real thing, build a fake for unit and handler tests, find a less-fake version to run in your Docker environment, and test that less-fake version.
Use an abstract base class for a relatively complex external dependency that has multiple operations, but a plain function is fine for a simple single-operation dependency.
Once you have more than one adapter, passing dependencies around manually becomes painful unless you adopt some form of dependency injection.

When improving an existing big ball of mud, first identify the problem you are trying to solve, whether the software is too hard to change, performance is unacceptable, or there are inexplicable bugs, because a clear goal helps prioritize the work and justify it to the team.

Complex changes to a system are an easier sell when linked to feature work, since a large delivery project makes the argument for a few weeks of foundational cleanup, a cost Bob calls the architecture tax.
To break apart a ball of mud, start by working out the system's use cases, treating each user-interface action or each cron or background job as a single use case, and give each an imperative name.

Create a single function or class per use case that orchestrates the work: start its own database transaction if needed, fetch required data, check preconditions, update the domain model, and persist changes, succeeding or failing as an atomic unit.
It is fine to have duplication in use-case functions, because it is better to duplicate some code in a few places than to have use-case functions calling one another in a long chain.

Pull data-access, orchestration, and I/O concerns such as sending email or writing files out of the domain model and up into the use-case functions, using abstraction techniques to keep the handlers unit-testable even when they perform I/O.

Building a system where you dot your way through a connected object graph via the ORM is easy and convenient but should be avoided, because each property access might trigger a database lookup, making performance hard to reason about.
Break apart a highly connected object graph by identifying aggregates and replacing direct references between objects with identifiers.

Have each use case update a single aggregate, where one handler fetches one aggregate from a repository, modifies its state, and raises resulting events; use a read model when you need data from elsewhere and avoid updating multiple aggregates in one transaction.

The Strangler Fig pattern builds a new system around the edges of an old one while keeping it running, gradually intercepting and replacing bits of old functionality until the old system does nothing and can be switched off.

Event interception moves functionality in three steps: raise events representing the changes in the system you want to replace, build a second system that consumes those events to build its own domain model, then replace the older system.

When deploying an event-driven system, start with a walking skeleton, a first production deployment that just logs its input, because it forces you to tackle all the infrastructural questions and start working in production.
Recommend domain modeling as the first step when carving a new system out of an overgrown one, because in such systems engineers, product owners, and customers no longer speak the same language.
These patterns are broad-brush building blocks rather than battle-hardened production code, and adopting them gives new ways to shoot yourself in the foot, so they should be applied with care.

Years of adding hacks and workarounds to a broken model eventually catch up and force a full rewrite, and a bizarre modeling rule is a symptom of engineering and business stakeholders drifting into different languages.

Use interactive collaborative modeling techniques such as event storming, CRC modeling, and event modeling to bring engineers and product owners together, because humans collaborate well through play and the goal is a shared ubiquitous language and agreement on where the complexity lies.

Treat a domain problem as a TDD kata, a lunchtime workshop, or a spike at the start of a project, because once you can demonstrate the value of modeling it is easier to argue for structuring the project to optimize for it.

Adopt these techniques incrementally rather than all at once; in an existing system, first build a service layer to keep orchestration in one place, which then makes it easier to push logic into the model and edge concerns like validation and error handling out to the entrypoints.

When extracting use cases from tangled code, copy and paste it into a new place and make that new code clean, then replace uses of the old code and finally delete the mess, accepting more duplication in the short term.

CQRS is optional: repositories with view-builder objects that fetch data and transform it into read models are fine, and when you hit a performance problem you can rewrite a view builder to use custom queries or raw SQL.

Prefer moving handler-invokes-handler interactions to a message bus rather than having use cases call one another directly, so that a finished use case raises an event and a handler in another aggregate-centered subdomain runs.

If a use case needs to update two aggregates atomically in one transaction, the consistency boundary is wrong and you should consider a new aggregate that wraps what changes together; if the second aggregate is only read, that is fine or can use a read model, and if the two updates need not share a transaction, split them into two handlers linked by a domain event.

View models can carry complex logic such as permissions and authorization and sometimes need extensive unit tests, so split a view builder, which is easy to test with mocked data, from a view fetcher.

Aggregates, domain events, and dependency inversion predate microservices and are ways to control complexity in large systems, so microservices are not required, although a well-modeled set of use cases is relatively easy to move to its own service later.
Reliable messaging is hard, and Redis pub/sub is not reliable and should not be used as a general-purpose messaging tool, since you cannot have exactly-once delivery.

Splitting work into small, focused transactions that fail independently requires monitoring to know when a transaction fails and tooling to replay events, which is eased by using a transaction-log message broker such as Kafka or EventStore, or the Outbox pattern.

Make handlers idempotent so that calling them repeatedly with the same message does not make repeated changes to state, because idempotency is a key reliability technique that lets you safely retry events when they fail.
Events will need to change their schema over time, so you must find a way to document your events and share their schema with consumers, for example using JSON schema and markdown.

Configure the application through environment variables per the 12-factor manifesto so the same code runs on a developer machine, on the containers, and across dev, staging, and production, and centralize access in a config module that uses functions rather than import-time constants so client code can modify the environment.

Do not let the config module become a dumping ground; keep config values immutable and modify them only via environment variables, and if you use a bootstrap script, make it the only place besides tests where config is imported.
In a Dockerfile, install things in order of how frequently they are likely to change, from system dependencies to Python dependencies to source, in order to maximize reuse of the Docker build cache.
Provide config defaults that let the code run on a developer's local machine, or alternatively fail hard on missing environment variables, particularly when a default would be insecure in production.
exception: prefer failing hard on missing env vars when a default would be insecure in production

statement: Keep application source in an src folder installed with an editable pip install via a minimal setup.py, which makes imports easy and keeps tests separate.

Because infrastructure concerns are decoupled from the domain model and service layer, swapping the storage backend, for example from a database to CSV files, is just a matter of writing new Repository and Unit of Work classes while reusing all of the domain-layer and service-layer logic.
Centralize the common developer and CI commands in a Makefile or an equivalent like Invoke, because unlike documentation a Makefile is code and so has less tendency to become out of date.
Minimize the number of Docker images, because splitting images per type of application code usually costs more in complexity and longer rebuild and CI times than it is worth.

A CSV-backed repository can present the same in-memory-collection illusion as a database-backed one, so reimplementing the Repository and Unit of Work over CSV files pares the CLI app down to reading orders and invoking the unchanged service layer.

Applying this architecture with Django is harder because its ORM has no equivalent of SQLAlchemy's classical mapper, so the ActiveRecord object and the domain model cannot be the same object and you must build a manual translation layer behind the repository.
condition: when using Django

statement: Django is designed for the sweet spot of easy CRUD apps with minimal boilerplate, so it starts to hinder once the app is no longer simple CRUD, and features like the Django admin become dangerous when the whole point of the app is complex rules around state changes because the admin bypasses them.
condition: when using Django

statement: In an existing Django app, adopt the Repository and Unit of Work patterns mainly for faster unit tests in the short term and for decoupling from Django and the database if you anticipate migrating, and adopt the Service Layer pattern when you see a lot of duplication in your views.
condition: when working in an existing Django app

statement: You can do DDD with Django models via the fat-models approach as long as the app is not too complex, but the community finds fat models hit their own scalability problems around interdependencies between apps, in which case extract a business-logic or domain layer between the views and forms and the models.
condition: when using Django

statement: Put a logic module into every Django app from day one to give business logic a home and keep forms, views, and models free of it, as a stepping-stone toward a decoupled domain model or service layer later.
condition: when using Django

statement: Validation is about creating preconditions: you test the inputs of an operation against criteria and exit with an error if they are invalid, and it is useful to separate preconditions into syntax, semantics, and pragmatics.

Validate syntax, meaning the shape and structure of incoming data such as required fields, types, and ranges, at the edge of the system, so that a message handler always receives only a well-formed message containing all required information.

Put syntactic validation on the message type itself, for example a declarative schema plus a from_json constructor, optionally with a helper that unifies field declaration and validation, at the trade-off of losing the static types on the dataclass.

Postel's Law, the robustness principle, says be liberal in what you accept and conservative in what you emit, so be strict when sending messages to other systems and as lenient as possible when receiving messages from them.

Do not over-validate opaque identifiers such as SKUs, order numbers, or phone numbers; treat them as strings so other systems can change their format whenever they like without affecting you, since it is not your system's business what the format is.

Follow the Tolerant Reader pattern: extract only the fields you care about, do minimal validation of them, ignore extra unknown fields, and resist sharing message definitions between systems, which keeps your system robust as other systems change.

The Tolerant Reader and Postel approach suits event-based integration between services you control because it allows their independent evolution, but if you run an API open to the public internet there may be good reasons to be more conservative about the inputs you allow.
exception: be more conservative for a public internet-facing API

statement: Validate at the edge so that requests are known to be valid before the domain model or use-case handlers see them, keeping the domain free of defensive checks, because invalid data wandering through the system is a time bomb that does more damage the deeper it gets.

The message bus is a good place for cross-cutting concerns such as validation, so entrypoints only get a message from the outside world and report success or failure, the bus validates and routes the message, and handlers focus solely on use-case logic.

When you receive an invalid message there is usually little to do but log the error and continue, so count how many messages a system receives and how many are processed, skipped, or invalid, and alert on spikes in bad messages.

Validate semantics, the meaningfulness of a message, at the message-handler or service layer using contract-based preconditions gathered in an ensure module, which keeps the main service-layer flow clean and declarative.

Apply messages idempotently with a precondition that uses the same Unit of Work as the main use-case logic to avoid concurrency bugs, and raise a SkipMessage for a message that cannot be processed but represents no incorrect behavior, such as a duplicate create.
Avoid putting business logic into precondition checks: as a rule of thumb, if a rule can be tested inside the domain model, then it should be tested in the domain model.

Locate each type of validation in the right place: validate syntax on the message classes, semantics in the service layer or on the message bus, and pragmatics in the domain model, where context-dependent business rules like having enough stock available naturally live.

Invest time in writing declarative helpers for validating incoming messages and applying preconditions to your handlers, because a nice declarative approach makes the codebase much cleaner and it is worth making boring code easy to maintain.

When talking about validation, be clear about which of the three kinds you mean, because validation means different things to different people: syntax is the structure of messages, semantics is their meaningfulness, and pragmatics is the business logic governing your response to them.
